C005.subject: Raising the minimum wage
C005.object: automation adoption rates among firms in high-elasticity local markets
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Raising the minimum wage automation adoption rates among firms in high-elasticity local markets]

[PATH:empirical] Quasi-experimental studies of minimum wage increases in local labor markets with high demand elasticity (e.g., fast-food industry in border counties) — These studies can directly measure changes in automation adoption (e.g., use of self-service kiosks, automated ordering systems) following minimum wage hikes, isolating the effect in markets where firms are most sensitive to labor costs.

[PATH:empirical] Firm-level survey data on technology investment decisions linked to state-level minimum wage changes — Longitudinal surveys of firms in low-skill sectors (e.g., retail, hospitality) can track whether wage increases correlate with accelerated adoption of labor-replacing technologies, controlling for other factors like productivity shocks.

[PATH:theoretical] Dynamic labor demand models incorporating automation as an endogenous response to wage floors — Calibrated models can simulate how different levels of minimum wage above market-clearing affect firm incentives to invest in automation, especially under varying elasticity assumptions, providing testable predictions for empirical validation.

scope.domain: low-skill labor markets with high labor demand elasticity

qualifier.context: effect is strongest when wage floor is set above market-clearing level

C006.subject: Raising the minimum wage
C006.object: employment for low-skill workers in high-elasticity local markets
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Raising the minimum wage employment for low-skill workers in high-elasticity local markets]

[PATH:empirical] Dube, A., Lester, T. W., & Reich, M. (2010). Minimum wage effects across state borders: Estimates using contiguous counties. Review of Economics and Statistics, 92(4), 945-964. — This study uses a quasi-experimental border discontinuity design to isolate minimum wage effects on low-skill employment. Replicating or extending this analysis to metropolitan areas with high labor demand elasticity (e.g., using industry mix or local labor supply measures) could directly test whether employment increases in those specific markets.

[PATH:empirical] Meer, J., & West, J. (2016). Effects of the minimum wage on employment dynamics. Journal of Human Resources, 51(2), 500-522. — This paper examines employment dynamics (e.g., hiring and separation rates) rather than static employment levels. For high-elasticity local markets, dynamic adjustments may reveal whether minimum wage increases stimulate hiring of low-skill workers or instead reduce job turnover. Panel data on metropolitan areas with high demand elasticity could be analyzed to assess this.

[PATH:literature] Neumark, D., & Wascher, W. (2007). Minimum wages and employment. Foundations and Trends in Microeconomics, 3(1–2), 1-182. — This comprehensive review synthesizes decades of empirical evidence and theoretical models. It can identify conditions under which minimum wage increases might raise employment in high-elasticity settings, such as monopsony power or efficiency wage effects, and highlight gaps in the literature that could be addressed with new data or methods.

scope.domain: low-skill labor markets with high labor demand elasticity

qualifier.geographic: United States metropolitan areas with high labor demand elasticity

C007.subject: Raising the minimum wage
C007.object: poverty rates among low-skill workers in markets with moderate to low elasticity
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Raising the minimum wage poverty rates among low-skill workers in markets with moderate to low elasticity]

[PATH:empirical] Empirical panel data studies comparing poverty rate changes in U.S. states with different minimum wage levels and low-skill employment elasticities (e.g., using CPS or SIPP data) — Directly tests the hypothesis by measuring net earnings changes and poverty outcomes across labor markets with varying demand elasticity, controlling for confounding factors.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of minimum wage effects on employment and earnings for low-skill workers (e.g., Doucouliagos & Stanley, 2009; updated reviews) — Synthesizes existing evidence to assess the condition that hours reduction is less than wage increase, and whether this holds in moderate-to-low-elasticity markets.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical labor market models incorporating monopsony power and heterogeneous worker productivity (e.g., Card & Krueger's model, or search-and-matching frameworks) — Provides formal predictions about when wage increases raise net earnings and reduce poverty, clarifying the elasticity threshold and market conditions required for the hypothesis to hold.

scope.domain: low-skill labor markets with moderate to low elasticity

qualifier.context: only when the resulting reduction in hours is less than the proportional wage increase, thereby increasing net earnings

C008.subject: Raising the minimum wage
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Raising the minimum wage total employment for low-skill workers]

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of minimum wage studies focusing on low-skill labor markets (e.g., Neumark & Wascher, Card & Krueger) — A comprehensive meta-analysis can synthesize findings across multiple studies to estimate the average effect on low-skill employment, especially in elastic labor markets, helping to confirm or refute the hypothesis.

[PATH:empirical] Quasi-experimental study using cross-state variation in minimum wage increases in the U.S. (e.g., difference-in-differences or event study) — Leveraging policy changes across states with varying labor demand elasticities provides causal estimates of employment effects for low-skill workers, directly testing the hypothesis under the specified scope conditions.

scope.domain: low-skill labor markets with moderate to high elasticity

qualifier.temporal: during periods of moderate to high labor demand elasticity
qualifier.geographic: in low-skill labor markets typical of developed economies with flexible wage structures
